book: 193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits

chapters.relation: Written in the voice of the GhostFacers mourning their slain intern Alan Corbett, the introduction presents the volume as their covert infiltration of 'the industry of philosophy.' It reports that philosophy derives from the Greek philosophia, 'loving wisdom,' and jokes that the philosophers it recruited all 'readily admitted that they knew nothing' yet kept pursuing it, with a running gag about whether knowledge itself might be a tulpa. It frames the following essays as the GhostFacers' manifesto of truth about what exists in the Supernatural universe, ghosts and demons included and the Winchester 'Wine-chesters' excluded.

Nathan Stout uses P.F. Strawson's account of moral responsibility through 'reactive attitudes' to ask when Sam and Dean are justified in killing what they hunt. Monsters sort into three groups: low-functioning animal killers like the wendigo and 'Heart''s werewolf Madison, intelligent but conscienceless 'antisocial' monsters like demons and leviathans, and 'moral monsters' like the cow-blood-drinking vampires of 'Bloodlust' and the kitsune Amy from 'The Girl Next Door,' who can understand and be motivated by moral reasons. Because Group 3 monsters are members of the moral community, Dean's 'if it's supernatural, we kill it' bigotry and his secret killing of Amy make the supposedly good hunters morally suspect, since killing a fellow member of the moral community ought to weigh on them.

Foresman and Tobienne deploy Aristotle's apparatus of essence and accident, the ten categories, and actuality versus potentiality to define the monster and explain the show's appeal. They test candidates against canon: whether hunting is essential or accidental to Sam after Azazel's kills, what John Winchester in 'Dead Man's Blood' treats as essential to vampire substance, and Madison's transformation in 'Heart' from actual human and potential werewolf into actual monster, concluding that monstrosity lies in thought and action rather than appearance, as the human-hunting but human Benders confirm. Tracing 'monster' to the Latin monstrum, a sign or omen, they argue monsters are monsters only through their relation to human self-importance, so our 'speciesist' prejudice is exactly why we love watching them hunted, and why we love Supernatural.

Shannon Ford reconstructs the Winchesters' ethics of killing: self-defense and defense of others justify lethal force, as when Sam kills Jeremy in 'Dream a Little Dream of Me' and Andy shoots Ansem to save Dean in 'Simon Said,' while Dean's refusal of Ruby's virgin-sacrifice spell in 'Jus in Bello' and sparing the disarmed Pa Bender mark lines they will not cross even when the math favors killing. Killing possessed innocents like Meg is treated as permissible only under necessity and with regret. The chapter then argues that once the brothers hunt to banish all demons from the world, their conflict is war rather than hunting, so just war theory (jus ad bellum and jus in bello) might license killings ordinary morality forbids, a slippage dramatized by Gordon's enjoyment of killing and Dean's unjustifiable killing of Amy.

Ralston and Applegate read the Winchesters' contested destiny through the free will debate: the angels' case for determinism runs from a cupid arranged to couple John and Mary, through Azazel's deal and Mary's death, to Zachariah and Michael's claim that 'free will is an illusion' and the brothers must say yes as vessels. Sartre supplies the response: with no pre-given essence, the Winchesters are radically free and responsible, Dean admirably resisting 'bad faith' while Sam's early rebellions are self-deceptive until he stops blaming family expectations. Hume's point that free choices must still flow from the agent's character and values grounds a two-stage model of free will used to argue that soulless Sam, lacking the moral filter of the soul, has more options but is less free and less responsible.

Foresman asks what would make Hell a justified punishment for the souls claimed by crossroads deals, like Mary, John, and Dean trading damnation to bring a loved one back to life. Using Joel Feinberg's expressive account of punishment, he argues that souls in Hell through stupid deals suffer mere bad consequences rather than punishment, because no message of moral condemnation reaches someone who never knew the rule. Bentham's utilitarian test fails to justify Hell, since a Hell nobody takes seriously deters nobody and nothing there is rehabilitated, and Kantian retributivism fails too because no finite wrong can deserve eternal torment, leaving Crowley's endless-queue Hell as at least better proportioned to desert.

Dena Hurst reads Heaven's civil war through Hobbes's Leviathan: with God absent there is no common power, so the angels fall into a state of nature that is a state of war, complete with natural equality, competition over the same prize, and glory-seeking, as when Zachariah's faction lets Lilith break the seals to force the Apocalypse. God ruled as sovereign by acquisition and proves 'a lousy king' not for demanding obedience but by vanishing without designating a successor, dissolving civil society and with it justice, since where there is no law there is no injustice. Meanwhile Hell under Crowley and the leviathans under Dick Roman display Hobbesian legitimacy from opposite directions: demons join by covenant-like contracts, making Hell a rough democracy, while the leviathans' unified hierarchy enacts the Leviathan itself.

Canode reads 'It's a Terrible Life' as Marx's alienation of labor: Dean Smith's corporate existence at Sandover Bridge & Iron is Zachariah's ruse, and the American dream, like the promise that one more hunt will finally let the brothers quit, is the ideology that keeps workers laboring for owners who profit from them. Sam and Dean become the proletariat and the angels the owners of the means of production, and their refusal of Heaven's plan enacts the Communist Manifesto's line that the bourgeoisie has forged the weapons of its own destruction. The closing meta-turn applies the critique to the audience: fans who watch, buy DVDs, and attend conventions are the bourgeoisie whose demand keeps the Winchesters hunting.

Brace applies Kant's prohibition on using persons merely as means to the women of Supernatural: Bobby helping willingly is not objectification, demonic possession and Azazel's forcing Ellen's gun to her own head are, and Zachariah's 'fornicate with women' pitch reduces women to objects. She reads Mary, Ellen, and Jo as warrior mothers whose duty and sacrifice, following Jean Bethke Elshtain, the brothers most respect, while Mill's utilitarianism explains the lovers (Jessica, Lisa, the djinn-dream Carmen) each brother sacrifices to the mission. The 'Jus in Bello' virgin-sacrifice debate exposes the tension, since Dean invokes Kantian respect yet ignores Nancy's free choice to die, and the killings of female monsters like Amy and Emma show objectification running in both directions.

Browning shows that 'Jus in Bello' is built from Romero's Night of the Living Dead: the besieged police station is a 'survival space' (a form he traces to Matheson's I Am Legend), Henricksen takes Ben's role and Nancy Barbra's, and the massed possessed townspeople mirror the shuffling zombie horde. Inside that space the show stages a clash of values, Ruby's utilitarian spell requiring Nancy's heart against Dean's absolute refusal to kill an innocent ('your choice is not a choice'), resolved by the rock-salt-and-exorcism plan that kills no one. The survival space works as a proving ground for its occupants' values, and the ending, where Lilith slaughters Nancy anyway, indicts the heroes' scruples and asks what the body count says about the viewers who enjoyed it.

Haas uses Dean's stubborn refusal to believe in God, even after meeting Castiel, escaping Hell, and visiting Heaven, to run through the problem of evil. Casey's challenge in 'Sin City' states the logical problem; the free-will theodicy answers it but falters before Supernatural's designed horrors like the rugaru, a creature God built to suffer an irresistible hunger that ends with it eating its spouse. Dean's real objection is the evidential problem, that the amount and severity of apparently pointless evil makes the omni-God unlikely, and neither a 'natural order' defense (Dick Roman humanely farming humans for food) nor John Hick's soul-making theodicy explains suffering far beyond what character formation requires.

Curry argues that angels like Anna and Castiel can reasonably be atheists, because a higher perspective confers no epistemic advantage about God: Anna admits only four angels have seen him and the rest 'take it on faith.' Aquinas's cosmological argument, illustrated by the endless causal chain behind the Impala, yields at most an uncaused first cause rather than an omnipotent, omnibenevolent one, and Paley's design argument, an Impala in the desert implies a designer, is undermined by Darwinian natural selection, which Castiel himself witnessed ('Don't step on that fish'). The free-will theodicy fails against natural evils like famine and childhood cancer, and the principle of parsimony tells angels to expect a natural explanation for their own existence, so Uriel's 'There is no will. No wrath. No God.' turns out to be rational.

Chaib takes Ruby's line that Hell is 'forgetting what you are' and reads God's character through early modern philosophy: Descartes' supremely real being and deceiving demon frame Castiel's delusion of godhood and Ruby's manipulation of Sam, Spinoza's denial that evil exists (it is 'inadequate knowledge') explains the comprehensible motives of Crowley and Lucifer, Berkeley's claim that things persist only because God perceives them makes a dead God an existential threat, and Kant's 'moral theism' rebuts dogmatic atheism. With Hegel and Fromm, Hell becomes self-forgetting and communion with God becomes self-knowledge achieved through knowing others, the opposite of Ruby's Hell. The chapter concludes via Locke that closing Hell's gates would deny once-human demons the redemption tied to our very idea of God, so the brothers' forgiving love, unlike Michael and Lucifer's rigidity, reflects God's nature.

Blackmon and Foresman ask what makes ghosts, spells, and holy water supernatural, rejecting definitions based on fiction, disbelief, or weirdness, and using Quine's point about the circularity of dictionary definitions to show lexicography cannot settle the question. Definitions keyed to current science or to the causal nexus fail because ghosts in Supernatural and in Hamlet causally interact, Bobby's ghost talks, moves objects, and possesses a maid, so the authors define the supernatural as what can on occasion transcend the world of material interaction. Descartes' interactionist substance dualism supplies the model: the cogito (even a djinn cannot make you falsely believe you exist), the pineal gland as the soul's point of causal contact, and a testable hypothesis that makes the supernatural scientifically investigable and implies that we, as spirits, are supernatural too.

Goguen reads the Winchesters through two masculine ideals: the warrior (Dean and Michael, chivalric protection culminating in Dean's 'protecting Sam... it's who I am') and the sovereign (Sam and Lucifer, whose freedom is analyzed with Isaiah Berlin's negative and positive liberty, with nods to Hobbes's absolute sovereign and Nietzsche's Übermensch). The show's stoic culture, where 'baring my soul like a freaking girl' is an insult, keeps the L-word unspoken, making Ellen's dying 'I will always love you, baby' to Jo a foil the brothers cannot match. Plato's Symposium, via Aristophanes' myth of split soulmates, and Aristotle's claim that the purest love is between virtuous male friends make sense of the 'psychotically, irrationally, erotically codependent' bond, and the chapter concludes that true masculinity requires embracing the seemingly supernatural: love.

Evolutionary biologist Graves applies naturalist method to the Supernatural universe: assume natural explanations first, as the Catholic Church does before granting an exorcism, and only posit the supernatural where naturalism fails. He builds a naturalistic phylogeny in which souls behave like genetic codes (50,000 new souls when Balthazar unsinks the Titanic), and demons, ghosts, and most monsters derive from human souls, which explains why mundane salt, iron, fire, and burned bones work on them, while pagan gods killable by wooden stakes and dog's blood are 'more akin to monsters' than gods. The framework yields rules and predictions about the Colt, holy water, and the Croatoan virus, and even suggests God and Death may be natural beings obeying laws lesser beings do not share.

holes.name: Reactive Attitudes (Freedom and Resentment)
holes.what: P.F. Strawson's account of moral responsibility, on which a being is a responsible member of the moral community just in case moral emotions like resentment and indignation are appropriate responses to it, as opposed to an objective attitude of management and control.
holes.why: Chapter 8's entire framework for deciding which monsters Sam and Dean may kill is Strawson's reactive attitudes, from soulless Sam to the 'moral monsters' of 'Bloodlust,' and neither the philosopher nor the concept exists in the taxonomy.

holes.name: Soul-Making Theodicy (Irenaean)
holes.what: John Hick's Irenaean theodicy, on which God allows evil and suffering because a world of adversity is a proving ground in which free but imperfect creatures forge virtuous, salvation-worthy souls.
holes.why: Chapter 19 devotes its final section to testing Hick's soul-making theodicy against Dean's world, arguing via the rugaru and the Winchesters' bloody moral growth that Supernatural contains far more suffering than soul-making could justify.

holes.name: John Hick
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of religion (1922-2012), author of 'An Irenaean Theodicy' and the soul-making response to the evidential problem of evil.
holes.why: Chapter 19 explicitly cites and applies Hick's theodicy at length as the last defense of God against Dean's evidential argument, and Hick is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Naturalism (naturalistic explanation)
holes.what: The view that natural phenomena are explained by other natural phenomena via the senses and the scientific method, so that supernatural explanations are admitted, if at all, only where naturalistic ones fail.
holes.why: Chapter 25's whole project is to naturalize Supernatural, treating souls as genetic codes and deriving a phylogeny of demons, ghosts, and monsters from human origins, and the taxonomy has no naturalism slug under knowledge-science-reality.
